name: Gödel Agent: A Self-Referential Agent Framework for Recursively Self-Improvement
authors: Xunjian Yin, Xinyi Wang, Liangming Pan, Li Lin, Xiaojun Wan, William Yang Wang (lead affiliation: Peking University; also UC Santa Barbara and University of Arizona)
venue: ACL 2025 (Long Papers), ACL Anthology 2025.acl-long.1354; first released as arXiv preprint 2410.04444 (Oct 2024)
reflection_type: verbal-self-critique over its own source code: the LLM introspects/reads its current runtime code and reasons ('thinking before acting') about whether and how to rewrite itself; the meta-optimization loop itself (not just task outputs) is the object of critique. Closest to a search-guided / self-referential code-rewriting variant of verbal self-critique rather than learned-critic or debate
feedback_source: environment-reward — a task utility function U(E, pi) computed on a validation set provides a real-valued performance score after each self-modification; supplemented by execution error traces/feedback (error-handling mechanism) and self-generated reasoning. No trained critic; feedback is the held-out validation accuracy/F1 signal
iteration_structure: iterative-refine via recursive self-improvement: the main loop is implemented as a recursive function (continue_improve) rather than a fixed iteration loop; each recursive depth the agent inspects/modifies its code and re-evaluates. Runs are organized as multiple independent self-improvement cycles (6 cycles, up to 30 iterations each) with reversion to a previous best when performance declines
reflection_object: agent's own code/architecture — Gödel Agent reads and rewrites its own runtime Python code via monkey patching, modifying both the task policy pi and the self-referential learning algorithm I (the meta-optimizer), including the code responsible for analysis and modification itself. It does NOT update model weights; the underlying LLM is fixed (though the paper proposes future fine-tuning of its own LLM as a direction)
requires_training: none — no gradient updates to the LLM; 'learning' is realized entirely by the (fixed) LLM rewriting its own runtime code/prompts guided by validation feedback. Despite the task's metadata tag of gradient_weight_update, the implemented method performs no weight updates (the paper lists self-LLM-finetuning only as future work)
reward_or_critic_model: verifiable reward — a task utility/evaluation function on a validation set (e.g., MGSM accuracy, DROP F1) supplies the scalar improvement signal; the LLM also acts as self-as-judge when deciding which code modifications to keep. No separately trained reward or retrospective model
distillation_target: model-weights — N/A; reflection is distilled into the agent's own rewritten code (its policy pi and meta-optimizer I) held in runtime memory, i.e., a self-modifying code artifact rather than episodic memory, a skill library, or model weights. The closest fitting categorical label is none-of-the-fixed-options; the persisted artifact is the evolved agent source code itself
emergent_vs_engineered: prompt/scaffold-engineered — the self-referential rewriting behavior is engineered via a goal prompt that grants the agent privileges to self-modify plus an initial scaffold (self_inspect, interact, self_update, continue_improve actions, thinking, error-handling, code/LLM-calling tools). It is not RL-emergent (no R1-style 'aha'); the LLM's reasoning drives the engineered self-modification loop
memory_type: short-term/scratchpad — the agent operates on its own runtime memory (Python local/global variables, classes, functions) which it inspects and overwrites; carried error information across steps acts as a working scratchpad. No dedicated long-term episodic store or skill library; the 'memory' is the live mutable code/state of the agent itself
memory_persistence: within-episode / cross-episode — state and code changes persist across recursive iterations within a self-improvement cycle (cross-iteration within an optimization run) and the optimized agent is saved and reused at test time; it is not a cross-session production memory system
memory_curation_mechanism: overwrite/evolution (self-relinking) — the agent dynamically rewrites its own code in runtime memory (add/replace/remove logic via monkey patching); when a modification degrades performance it can revert to a previous optimal algorithm, and error traces are carried forward. Curation is the agent's own self-modification rather than an external append/summarize policy
error_localization_granularity: block-level (code) / holistic — feedback is primarily outcome-level (validation score after a modification), but the agent localizes changes to specific code blocks/modules of its own logic that it chooses to rewrite; execution errors are localized via error traces (and, in case studies, an error-trace library) to the failing code segment
intra_task_vs_inter_task: inter-task — Gödel Agent transfers/optimizes its agent design over many validation instances within a task to produce an optimized agent for held-out test instances (a task-level self-optimizer), analogous to Reflexion/ExpeL-style inter-task improvement rather than refining a single answer in-flight
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: avoidance-only with reversion — failed or performance-degrading self-modifications are detected via validation feedback and the agent reverts to a prior best or adjusts its optimization direction in subsequent iterations; it does not correct an in-flight task trajectory (mid-trajectory recovery is not the mechanism). Error-handling lets it skip a crashing modification and carry the error forward
task_domains: QA/reasoning, math, science, and reading comprehension (described by authors as coding, science, math, and reasoning / multitasking); plus a Game of 24 reasoning case study
benchmarks: DROP (reading comprehension, F1), MGSM (multilingual math, accuracy), MMLU (multi-task, accuracy), GPQA (graduate-level science, accuracy); Game of 24 used as a case study
headline_result: With GPT-3.5 under matched constraints (Gödel-base, closed-book), Gödel Agent meets or beats the SOTA automated-design baseline Meta Agent Search on all four benchmarks, most notably +~11% on MGSM (64.2% vs 53.4%). Scores: DROP F1 80.9, MGSM 64.2%, MMLU 70.9%, GPQA 34.9%. The unconstrained Gödel-free variant (allowed to call stronger models e.g. GPT-4o) reaches DROP 90.5, MGSM 90.6%, MMLU 87.9%, GPQA 55.7%
baselines: Hand-designed: Chain-of-Thought, CoT-SC (Self-Consistency), Self-Refine, LLM-Debate, Step-back Abstraction, Quality-Diversity, Role Assignment. Automated agent design (main comparison): Meta Agent Search (Hu et al. 2024, ADAS). Also compared against a random-sampling baseline (Appendix F)
gains_vs_baseline: vs the strongest baseline Meta Agent Search (GPT-3.5, matched setting): MGSM +10.8pp (64.2 vs 53.4), DROP F1 +1.5 (80.9 vs 79.4), MMLU +1.3pp (70.9 vs 69.6), GPQA +0.3pp (34.9 vs 34.6) — large gain on math/reasoning, comparable elsewhere. Authors also report faster convergence and lower compute than Meta Agent Search (Appendix D). The unconstrained Gödel-free version far exceeds all baselines (e.g., MGSM 90.6%) largely by spontaneously calling stronger models
compute_cost_profile: Inference/test-time-compute method (no training/gradient cost). Optimization budget: 6 independent self-improvement cycles per task, up to 30 self-improvement iterations per cycle on the validation set, each iteration involving LLM calls for reasoning + code rewriting + a validation evaluation; authors report fewer iterations and lower computational cost than Meta Agent Search (Appendix D). Exact API-call/token multiplier not stated numerically
known_limitations: (1) As the first self-referential agent it must build all task code autonomously, so it is not compared to heavily-engineered systems like OpenDevin and is not expected to beat them; experiments only demonstrate feasibility. (2) As the self-modified system grows complex it may need exponentially more intelligence to understand itself, so a fully self-referential system can lose self-referential capability as it evolves (Yampolskiy 2015); the breakdown point is unstudied. (3) Cannot reliably innovate beyond SOTA algorithms given current LLM limits (e.g., does not surpass Tree-of-Thought on Game of 24). (4) Robustness: in 100 MGSM trials it occasionally makes erroneous changes — 4% unexpected terminations, 92% temporary performance drops, and 14% of trials ultimately fail (worse than the initial policy). (5) Safety concerns from unconstrained self-modification (proposed mitigations: sandboxing, constrained modifications)
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: env-reward — improvement depends on a task utility/validation-set evaluation function (and execution error feedback), i.e., environment reward signal from a held-out validation set rather than unaided intrinsic self-judgment. It is not pure intrinsic self-verification (validation labels/metric provide the signal), but it is not full per-instance ground-truth oracle access during test either
self_correction_efficacy: net-positive but task-dependent — under matched settings it improves over hand-designed agents and matches/beats Meta Agent Search, with the largest gains on reasoning/math; however 14% of MGSM optimization trials end worse than the initial policy and it cannot exceed strong existing algorithms (e.g., ToT) on Game of 24. Final task performance usually exceeds the initial baseline thanks to reversion to prior best when performance declines
calibration_effect: not-measured (the paper reports task accuracy/F1 and optimization robustness statistics, not confidence calibration or overconfidence/'reasoning tax')
failure_attribution_capability: n/a — not a failure-attribution method; it uses execution error traces and validation-score drops to decide which self-modifications to keep or revert, but does not classify failure modes via a taxonomy or attribute responsibility across agents/steps
failure_mode_addressed: Targets the design-space limitation of static hand-designed and fixed meta-learning agents (inability to search the whole agent design space). Its own observed failure modes (cross-link to error-loop / self-modification instability): error-loop / crash from modifying the recursive-improvement module (4% terminations), temporary performance regressions (92%), and net-negative optimization runs (14%); mitigated by error handling and reversion rather than eliminated
dataset_or_benchmark_released: No new dataset/benchmark released; evaluation reuses existing benchmarks (DROP, MGSM, MMLU, GPQA, Game of 24) following the setup of Hu et al. (2024). Open-source code released at https://github.com/Arvid-pku/Godel_Agent
builds_on: Gödel machine (Schmidhuber 2003) and recursive self-improvement theory (Good 1966; Schmidhuber 1987; Wang 2018; Yampolskiy 2015; Steunebrink & Schmidhuber 2012); Meta Agent Search / ADAS (Hu et al. 2024) as the automated-agent-design predecessor and main baseline; self-taught optimizer / STOP (Zelikman et al. 2023); fine-tuning-based self-improvement (Havrilla et al. 2024; Qu et al. 2024 RISE; Kumar et al. 2024); reflection/self-refine agent methods (Shinn et al. 2024 Reflexion; Madaan et al. 2024 Self-Refine); monkey patching (Bimal 2012)
extended_by_or_inspired: Huxley-Gödel Machine (Wang, Piekos, ... Schmidhuber 2025); Polaris: A Gödel Agent Framework for Small Language Models through Experience-Abstracted Policy Repair (Kakade et al. 2026, Highly Influenced); CLMC: Code-Level Metacognition for LLM Agents (Jian et al. 2025, ICDM); AgentBreeder (Rosser & Foerster 2025); SwarmAgentic (Zhang et al. 2025, EMNLP); Agentic Neural Networks (Ma et al. 2025); Weak-for-Strong / W4S (Nie et al. 2025); JudgeFlow (Ma et al. 2026); also discussed alongside A Self-Improving Coding Agent (Robeyns et al.) and Live-SWE-agent (Xia et al.)
citation_count: 18 (Semantic Scholar, as of June 2026; Google Scholar count is likely higher)
reasoning_model_native: no — evaluated with GPT-3.5 (and optionally GPT-4o calls in the unconstrained variant); it engineers a self-modification scaffold around a standard (non-reasoning-specialized) LLM rather than relying on o1/R1-style built-in reflection. The authors note future LLM capability gains would unlock more innovative self-optimization
on_policy_distillation_link: Weak link — Gödel Agent does not distill on-policy rollouts into weights; its analogue of policy improvement is on-policy code/prompt rewriting evaluated against a validation utility (a non-gradient, test-time-compute form of self-improvement). The paper frames self-code-modification as an executable, more diverse form of test-time computing rather than on-policy distillation into model weights
sample_efficiency: Per-task optimization uses 6 self-improvement cycles with up to 30 iterations each (so a few hundred LLM-reasoning + validation evaluations per task); authors report it converges in fewer iterations and at lower compute than Meta Agent Search (Appendix D), though no precise sample-efficiency multiplier is given
